target.name: Galmaemot Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: On a hill above the shore at Ocheon in Boryeong, looking out over the West Sea, stands a church roofed in the shape of a shell: Our Lady of Victory. On the sand below this small and beautiful church, on 30 March 1866, five men were beheaded at the military execution ground. They were Bishop Marie-Nicolas-Antoine Daveluy, fifth Vicar Apostolic of Korea, Frs. Pierre Aumaître and Martin-Luc Huin, the lay leader St. Luke Hwang Seok-du, and St. Joseph Jang Ju-gi of the seminary. Open the church doors and the stained glass behind the altar holds the eye. Slide that glass door aside and the West Sea opens out before you, the same sea the saints looked upon last.
target.history: All five martyred in the Byeongin Persecution of 1866, including Bishop Daveluy, were canonized. They were brought this far from the capital for execution because a royal selection of a consort for King Gojong was expected, and executions near Seoul were to be avoided.

target.name: Ganggyeong Church
target.description: At Ganggyeong in Nonsan, a village on an inlet of the Geum River, St. Andrew Kim Taegon began his first ministry on Korean soil. On 12 October 1845, Bishop Jean-Joseph Ferréol, Fr. Daveluy and Fr. Kim brought their boat ashore at Ganggyeong harbour and stayed about a month in the house of a believer named Gu Sun-o, ministering from there. The bishop remained in hiding for more than two months, carrying out his first duties as Vicar Apostolic of Korea. The present church, completed in 1961, combines pointed arches with modern construction and was listed as Registered Cultural Heritage No. 650 in 2015. In 2019 a memorial hall was added, modelled on the church in Shanghai where Fr. Kim was ordained.
target.history: Where St. Andrew Kim Taegon and Bishop Ferréol landed in 1845 and began the first ministry. The church completed in 1961 is Registered Cultural Heritage No. 650.

target.name: Gongseri Shrine Church
target.description: Cross the Asan Bay embankment, climb a low hill, and three ancient trees some 350 years old greet you first. Beyond them rises a Gothic spire in red brick. Built on the site of a Joseon-era warehouse that held the tax grain of forty villages, this church was completed in 1922 and is a jewel of Korea's early modern architecture. In spring the cherry trees along the approach settle like clouds, and the moss phlox on the hill becomes a pink sea. During the Korean War the eighth pastor, Fr. Emile Bulteau, refused to flee, saying a shepherd could not leave his flock.
target.history: Chosen in 2005 by the Korea Tourism Organization as the most beautiful church in Korea. Gothic church completed in 1922, with three martyrs of the Byeongin Persecution interred here. Fr. Bulteau was abducted and martyred during the Korean War.

target.name: Nambangje Shrine
target.description: In Sinchang-myeon in Asan, in a village named for an embankment bent like a hook, a willow more than two hundred years old bears witness to the early settlement here. St. Peter Jo Hwa-seo, who came from this village, fled here after his father was martyred in the Gihae Persecution. He went on to serve Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop as horseman and altar server, accompanying him on his ministry across the country. His son, St. Joseph Jo Yun-ho, lived in deep faith, and when father and son were arrested together in 1866 he refused every inducement to recant and chose martyrdom. Both died at Jeonju on 13 December that year. In 2016, on the 150th anniversary of their martyrdom, a conical memorial was raised to them and to 36 martyrs of the Sinchang area.
target.history: The village where Sts. Peter Jo Hwa-seo and Joseph Jo Yun-ho grew up. Father and son were martyred together at Jeonju in 1866. A memorial was erected in 2016 for the 150th anniversary.

target.name: Darakgol Shrine
target.description: In the mountains of Hwaseong-myeon in Cheongyang lies the birthplace of Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop, known as the martyr of sweat, and of his father St. Francis Choe Gyeong-hwan. It was one of the earliest Catholic villages, formed when Choe In-ju settled in this remote valley in 1791 to escape persecution. St. Francis died in prison in 1839 from the effects of torture during the Gihae Persecution, and his wife Maria Yi Seong-nye was martyred the following year. Local tradition holds that the bodies of those martyred at the Hongju government office during the Byeongin Persecution of 1866 were secretly buried here under cover of night. Before the rows of graves of these unnamed martyrs, a memorial chapel was built in 2008, and in 2019 a shrine museum honouring Fr. Choe Yang-eop.
target.history: Birthplace of St. Francis Choe Gyeong-hwan and his son Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop. An early Catholic village formed from 1791. The shrine museum opened in 2019.

target.name: Daeheung Bongsusan Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: Beside the old government office grounds at Daeheung-myeon in Yesan stands a reconstruction of a Joseon-era prison. Here, during the Sinyu Persecution of 1801, Blessed Peter Kim Jeong-deuk and his cousin Blessed Andrew Kim Gwang-ok, who had shared their faith as brothers, were arrested together. The magistrate offered to spare them if they would resume the ancestral rites, but they would not bend, saying they would proclaim God's word even if they had to hide in the mountains. Executed separately, one at Daeheung and one at Yean, they clasped hands just before and said they would meet again in heaven the next day. They were martyred together on the 17th day of the seventh lunar month of 1801. Both were beatified during Pope Francis's visit to Korea in 2014.
target.history: Where Blessed Peter Kim Jeong-deuk and his cousin Blessed Andrew Kim Gwang-ok were each executed during the Sinyu Persecution of 1801. The old Daeheung prison has been reconstructed. Beatified in 2014.
target.addressRomanized: 105-3 Dongseo-ri, Daeheung-myeon, Yesan-gun, Chungcheongnam-do (beside the Daeheung magistracy)

target.name: Deoksan Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: At Deoksan-myeon in Yesan, on a slope of Gayasan, lies the tomb of Prince Namyeon, father of the Heungseon Daewongun. In May 1868 the German merchant Ernst Oppert attempted to rob this tomb in order to force a trade agreement, and failed. The affair hardened the Daewongun's suspicion of Western powers and of Catholicism, and drove the Byeongin Persecution to greater severity. In its wake a considerable number of believers in the Deoksan area are said to have been seized and martyred. The shrine today holds the remains of unnamed martyrs and of the faithful who went before, and asks the visitor to consider how a single incident can fan the fire of persecution.
target.history: Near the site of Oppert's 1868 attempt to rob Prince Namyeon's tomb, an incident that intensified the Byeongin Persecution. The remains of unnamed martyrs of the Deoksan area are interred here.

target.name: Doanggol Shrine
target.description: In Naesan-myeon in Buyeo, in a valley once called Dowongok for its many peach trees, a Catholic village formed through the missionary work of Ludovico Yi Jon-chang. Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop, the second Korean priest, reported on nine months of ministry here in 1850, writing that he often saw the terrible poverty of the villagers, who suffered taxes and persecution even at the hands of family and neighbours. During the Byeongin Persecution of 1866, John O and John Kim Sul-jang and others were martyred at Galmaemot. A house of prayer was blessed in 2011, and that December a stone was raised marking the beatification of Fr. Choe Yang-eop. A walking pilgrimage route, retracing the paths of the persecution years, runs from here to Saptigo Shrine nearby.
target.history: The Catholic village on which Fr. Choe Yang-eop reported after nine months of ministry in 1850. John O and others were martyred at Galmaemot during the Byeongin Persecution of 1866.

target.name: Baenadeuri Shrine
target.description: On the Sapgyo River in Yesan, this village took its name from the boats needed to cross it whenever the river flooded. Blessed Martin In Eon-min, born into the gentry, came to the faith through his connection with Hwang Sa-yeong and was baptized in Seoul by Fr. James Zhou Wenmo. Arrested at Gongju during the Jeongsa Persecution of 1797, interrogated at Cheongju and transferred to Haemi, he was beaten to death on 9 January 1800 at the age of sixty-three. In 1817 officers from the Haemi government office raided this village and seized twenty or thirty believers; Peter Min Cham-ji and his sister-in-law Anna among them chose to die in prison rather than recant. Blessed Martin In Eon-min was beatified with 123 others in 2014.
target.history: Associated with the martyrdom of Blessed Martin In Eon-min (1737–1800). Many were martyred after the Haemi authorities raided the village in 1817. Beatified in 2014.

target.name: Sanmakgol and Jageunjae Shrine
target.description: In Pangyo-myeon in Seocheon, this was a refuge deep in the mountains where the faithful hid after the Gihae Persecution of 1839. Bishop Daveluy and Fr. Stanislas Féron made it a base for their ministry, and St. Luke Hwang Seok-du spent a decade in this valley in penance and reparation before the Byeongin Persecution. Mass graves of unnamed believers remained scattered here until road construction covered them in concrete in 1994. Research by Dr. Seo Jong-tae in 2010 brought their significance back to light, and Fr. Jeong Seong-yong laid out a memorial space, fourteen Stations of the Cross, and a 3.5-kilometre pilgrimage route linking the associated sites.
target.history: The refuge where St. Luke Hwang Seok-du spent a decade before the Byeongin Persecution. Site of mass graves of unnamed martyrs, rediscovered in 2010.

target.name: Sapti Shrine
target.description: On the boundary between Buyeo and Boryeong, in a mountain village beyond the Sapti pass, traces of St. Luke Hwang Seok-du remain. He brought his family here from Gwanpyeong in Chungcheongbuk-do in the 1850s, and would visit the village from time to time to teach the catechism and encourage the faithful, until he was martyred at Galmaemot on 30 March 1866 during the Byeongin Persecution. Relatives secretly recovered his body and buried it here; when this was discovered, some were themselves put to death. In 1962 an earthenware jar holding a crucifix, a statue of the Virgin and a rosary was unearthed at this spot, and is now kept at the museum of Jeoldusan Martyrs' Shrine. Restoration began in 2016, and in 2018 Buyeo County erected a cross and a memorial space.
target.history: The refuge where St. Luke Hwang Seok-du's family settled. Relics were unearthed here in 1962 and are now held at the Jeoldusan museum. Restored between 2016 and 2018.

target.name: Seojitgol Shrine
target.description: In Misan-myeon in Boryeong, a tobacco field holds the story of martyrs' remains that wandered the world for nearly a hundred and fifty years. On Good Friday, 30 March 1866, Bishop Daveluy, Frs. Aumaître and Huin, and the lay leader St. Joseph Jang Ju-gi were executed on the sands at Galmaemot, along with some five hundred of the faithful. Buried at first near the execution ground, their remains were moved that May to Opogol, and in July carried by boat here to Seojitgol, where they stayed fifteen years and six months. From here they went on in turn to Nagasaki in Japan in 1882, to the Yongsan seminary in 1894, to the crypt of Myeongdong Cathedral in 1900, and to Jeoldusan Martyrs' Shrine in 1967. In 2013 an outdoor altar of fifty tons of obsidian, carved with the four martyrs' names, was dedicated and the shrine laid out.
target.history: Where the remains of Bishop Daveluy and three other martyrs lay for fifteen years and six months between 1866 and 1882. The shrine was laid out in 2013.

target.name: Seonggeosan Shrine
target.description: Near the summit of Seonggeosan at about 500 metres, seven Catholic villages were scattered across these slopes from the 1860s to the 1920s. During the Byeongin Persecution, twenty-three people were martyred from six of the surrounding villages. At the site of the Sohakgol village, three thatched houses have been rebuilt to show how such a village once looked. In spring and autumn the wildflowers and the turning leaves make this a mountain shrine that pilgrims say they want to return to once they have come.
target.history: The site of mountain Catholic villages at about 500 metres; twenty-three were martyred from six of the seven villages. Connected to the family of Fr. Choe Yang-eop, Korea's second priest, whose uncle lived in the Seodeokgol village.

target.name: Solmoe Shrine
target.description: At Ugang-myeon in Dangjin, in the middle of the Naepo plain, a low rise is thick with pines. Solmoe means exactly that: pine hill. Under these pines, in 1821, St. Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, was born. His was a family that gave martyrs across four generations, from his great-grandfather Kim Jin-hu and his great-uncle Kim Jong-han to his father Kim Je-jun. A boy of fifteen, Andrew left here for Macao, returned as the first Korean priest, and was martyred at Saenamteo at the age of twenty-five. In the yard before the restored birthplace stands a sculpture of Pope Francis at prayer, from his visit here in 2014.
target.history: Birthplace of St. Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest. His family produced martyrs across four generations. National Historic Site No. 529, with more than 400,000 visitors a year.

target.name: Surichigol Marian Shrine
target.description: Deep in a valley at Sinpung-myeon in Gongju, the small house of one devout family became the starting point of Marian devotion in Korea. On 2 November 1846, Bishop Ferréol founded here the Confraternity of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, the first Marian association in the country. In years when the faithful had to live in hiding, the depth of the valley and the cover it gave made it a place where they could gather. A sculpture of the Trinity was erected in 1990, a Way of the Seven Sorrows of Mary laid out in 1993, and in 1997 the motherhouse of the Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Mary of Mirinae moved here.
target.history: Where Bishop Ferréol founded Korea's first Marian association, the Confraternity of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, in 1846.

target.name: Silli Shrine
target.description: Where Bishop Daveluy, fifth Vicar Apostolic of Korea, lived in hiding and carried out his ministry. His residence survives, rebuilt as a thatched house. It was here that the bishop was arrested during the Byeongin Persecution before being martyred at Galmaemot in Boryeong. Known as the catacomb of Joseon, the shrine was extensively renewed in 2024, its walls lowered to make it a place of rest.
target.history: Where Bishop Daveluy lived in hiding and was arrested; known as the catacomb of Joseon. Starting point of the Beugeunae Pilgrimage Route, with walking pilgrimages held by the Diocese of Daejeon each May and October.

target.name: Yeosaul Shrine
target.description: The birthplace of Ludovico Yi Jon-chang, the Apostle of Naepo. Baptized in 1784 by Yi Seung-hun, the first Korean to be baptized, he went on to spread the faith throughout the Naepo region. He was martyred at the provincial office in Gongju during the Sinyu Persecution of 1801. Through his work, Naepo became the cradle of the Catholic Church in Korea.
target.history: Birthplace of Ludovico Yi Jon-chang, the Apostle of Naepo. The starting point from which the faith spread through the Naepo region; he was martyred in the Sinyu Persecution of 1801.

target.name: Wonmeori Shrine
target.description: At Sinpyeong-myeon in Dangjin, this village took the name Wonmeori, meaning head of the bank, from the way it became an island at high tide. From the 1790s the faithful settled along the Sapgyo River here, making their living boiling salt and firing earthenware. Mark Bak Seon-jin and his son Matthias Bak Tae-jin were arrested in 1868 and taken to Suwon, where the son, broken by torture, recanted for a time; but he repented, and fifteen days later chose martyrdom together with his father. The two, aged thirty-three and fifty-two, were first laid at Sinpyeong Church, and in 2009 their remains were returned here to the old burial ground at Wonmeori.
target.history: Mark Bak Seon-jin and his son Matthias Bak Tae-jin were martyred at Suwon in 1868. Their remains were moved to Wonmeori in 2009.

target.name: Jeongsan Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: At Jeongsan-myeon in Cheongyang, a pedlar of earthenware who carried the Gospel from place to place gave his final witness. Blessed Paul Yi Do-gi had fled over Chilgapsan and settled here, teaching the catechism in secret as he went about selling his pots, until the Jeongsa Persecution of 1798, when at the age of fifty-four he was taken to the Jeongsan government office and severely interrogated. When the magistrate dangled an official post before him to make him recant, he answered that he could not betray God even if he were given the whole district of Jeongsan. Near the Jeongsan township office today, this spot recalls the resolve of one layman who carried the faith with nothing but his earthenware.
target.history: The site of the Jeongsan government office where Blessed Paul Yi Do-gi (1743–1798) was interrogated and martyred during the Jeongsa Persecution of 1798.
target.addressRomanized: 496-1 Seojeong-ri, Jeongsan-myeon, Cheongyang-gun, Chungcheongnam-do (near the township office)

target.name: Jiseok-ri Shrine
target.description: At Chunghwa-myeon in Buyeo, the home village of two martyr saints. St. Peter Son Seon-ji, as a lay leader, carried the consolation of faith even to fellow believers held in prison; and St. Bartholomew Jeong Mun-ho, born into the gentry, is said to have gone gladly to his death, saying he was going that day to sit the state examination in heaven. The two were beheaded together at Supjeongi in Jeonju during the Byeongin Persecution of 1866. The memorial and outdoor altar raised here by Hongsan parish in 1988 were renewed in 2014 with interpretive signs and a car park.
target.history: Home village of Sts. Peter Son Seon-ji and Bartholomew Jeong Mun-ho. Martyred together at Supjeongi in Jeonju in 1866, canonized in 1984.

target.name: Jinsan Shrine
target.description: At Jinsan-myeon in Geumsan, the home village of the first two martyrs of the Korean Church. Following the papal prohibition of ancestral rites, St. Paul Yun Ji-chung and his cousin St. James Gwon Sang-yeon burned the ancestral tablets and held Yun's mother's funeral according to Catholic rite. When this was discovered in 1791 they were denounced as unfilial sons, and on 8 December that year they were beheaded outside the south gate of Jeonju. This Jinsan Incident became the spark of the Sinhae Persecution. In time the scattered faithful gathered again into a parish, which passed from the Diocese of Jeonju to the Diocese of Daejeon in 1980 and was raised in 2009 from a small mission station to a pilgrimage church. The two martyrs were canonized in 2014.
target.history: Home village of Sts. Paul Yun Ji-chung and James Gwon Sang-yeon, the first martyrs of the Korean Church. The Jinsan Incident of 1791 triggered the Sinhae Persecution; canonized in 2014.

target.name: Daeheung-dong Catholic Church
target.description: The form is of two hands joined toward heaven. When it was completed in 1962, the tallest building in Daejeon was a church. Its 49.8-metre bell tower still stands at the centre of the old downtown, holding its place while the city grew up around it. The canopy at the front makes it easy to pass by, but look up and twelve apostles in relief keep watch over the church, and above them is stained glass by the painter Yi Nam-gyu, who learned the traditional technique in Austria. Past the main gate, beneath the pines, a Pietà stands quietly: a mother holding her son.
target.history: Completed in 1962; Registered Cultural Heritage No. 43 (listed 2014). A landmark of early modern architecture in Daejeon's old downtown and the tallest building in the city when it was built.

target.name: Hapdeok Church
target.description: At Hapdeok-eup in Dangjin, a red-brick church with twin towers looks out over the Naepo plain. Founded in 1890 as the Yangchon mission station in Yesan, the parish moved to this site in 1899 and took the name Hapdeok; the present brick church was completed in 1929 under Fr. Perrin. In 1950, in the midst of the Korean War, Fr. Perrin was arrested and martyred, and the layman Yun Bok-su and the altar server Song Sang-won lost their lives with him. A memorial to them stands in the churchyard. Silli Shrine, where Bishop Daveluy lived in hiding, is close by, and the two are well visited together.
target.history: Founded in 1890, church completed in 1929 (Chungcheongnam-do Monument No. 145). Fr. Perrin and two others were martyred during the Korean War.

target.name: Haemi Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: One kilometre west of Haemi Fortress in Seosan. Beneath this quiet ground among the fields lie more than a thousand martyrs whose names were never recorded. When the Byeongin Persecution began in 1866, believers seized across Chungcheong Province were brought to Haemi Fortress. They were imprisoned, tortured, and finally buried alive here on the banks of the Haemi stream. As they faced death they cried out Jesus, Mary, which the villagers heard as yeosu meori, and so the place came to be called Yeosutgol. In 2014 Pope Francis came here to honour the unnamed martyrs. Between the church seating seven hundred, the burial ground holding the martyrs' remains, and Jindumbeong where the executions were carried out, a single circuit of the shrine conveys both the cruelty of the late Joseon persecutions and the grandeur of the faith that met them.
target.history: The largest martyrdom site of the Byeongin Persecution of 1866. An estimated 1,000 or more martyrs, including 179 whose names are known. Visited by Pope Francis in 2014 for the closing Mass of Asian Youth Day.

target.name: Hongju Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: In the centre of Hongseong, the whole of the old Hongju fortress town, seat of a wide Joseon-era jurisdiction, was stained with the blood of martyrs. The magistrate's hall where believers were interrogated, the prison that held more than a hundred at a time, the execution ground on the Wolgye stream, the mass graves where two waters meet: across three periods from 1791 into the 1870s, 212 martyrs have been identified by name, and counting those who left no record the number is thought to exceed a thousand. During Pope Francis's visit to Korea in 2014, four people from Hongseong were beatified: Blessed Peter Won Si-jang, Blessed Francis Bang, Blessed Laurence Bak Chwi-deuk and Blessed Simon Hwang Il-gwang.
target.history: The whole of the Joseon-era Hongju fortress town was a place of martyrdom. 212 martyrs identified by name, with the true number estimated at over 1,000. Four were beatified in 2014.

target.name: Hwangmusil Shrine
target.description: On low hills at the boundary of Dangjin and Yesan stood a Catholic village that held to the faith through successive persecutions from 1791 to 1868. With Silli, it was a base where missionaries of the Paris Foreign Missions Society lived and ministered, and it keeps the traces of several French priests: Fr. Joseph Maistre, who founded an orphanage and the seminary at Baeron; Fr. Landre, who died here; and Fr. Huin, who was martyred. Some seventy martyrs are said to have come from this area alone. Forgotten for a time after the graves were moved in 1970, the site was designated a starting point for youth pilgrimages in 2008 and came back to life with the beatification of Blessed Francis Yi Bo-hyeon in 2014.
target.history: A Catholic village that endured successive persecutions from 1791 to 1868. A ministry base for Paris Foreign Missions Society priests, with some seventy martyrs from the area.

target.name: Hwangsaebawi Martyrdom Shrine
target.description: Just before the Geum River as you leave central Gongju, on a hill facing Gongsanseong Fortress, a martyrs' tower rises 13.8 metres. For about a century from 1791, Catholics seized across Chungcheong Province were brought to the provincial office at Gongju and executed on this hill. The names of 248 martyrs are known. Among them, St. Thomas Son Ja-seon, ordered by the magistrate to bear witness to his faith by biting his own flesh, did so without hesitation. In the stone-grave chapel beneath the tower the 248 names are inscribed, and the twelve pillars of light in the plaza serve both as gravestones for the unnamed martyrs and as a symbol of the twelve apostles.
target.history: The largest martyrdom site in Chungcheongnam-do, in use for about a century from 1791 into the 1890s. 248 martyrs have been identified, from Chungcheong, Jeolla, Gyeonggi and elsewhere.
